notes:
I've put together notes for vv. 1, 4, 6–8, 12–21. I didn't get commentary that deals specifically with vv. 2–3, 5 or 9–11, so those verses are left out. I also found nothing from the Catholic, Orthodox, modern-scholarship (bibleodyssey.org, netbible.org) or prosperity/word-of-faith sources, so the "other views" section is short.

**Verses 1–12 as a whole (the borders)**
- Guzik says these place names mattered to the people who would live there, and they show the land was a real place, not a symbolic or spiritual inheritance. Meyer (quoted by Guzik) adds that Judah, the tribe of the future kings, would be toughened by "constant watchfulness against the foe and long-continued fighting." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-15-16-17/
- Clarke and William MacDonald (quoted on Precept Austin) note that many of the places can no longer be located exactly. Clarke says this does not affect the truth of the account. MacDonald says the details still matter to God and are full of spiritual lessons. https://www.preceptaustin.org/joshua-15-commentary

**v. 1**
- Precept Austin's own note says Joshua describes Judah's borders carefully because it was the first and most numerous tribe, the tribe of the kings, and the tribe the Messiah would come from. The territory later proved too large, so land was taken out of it for Simeon and Dan. https://www.preceptaustin.org/joshua-15-commentary
- Woudstra (on Precept Austin) says Judah being listed first points ahead to its later prominence and to the "scepter" of Genesis 49:10. Stephen Grant, citing Howard, notes that Judah's border description is the most detailed of any tribe's. https://www.preceptaustin.org/joshua-15-commentary

**v. 4**
- Madvig (on Precept Austin) points out that Judah's southern border closely matches the southern border of Canaan given in Numbers 34:3–5. https://www.preceptaustin.org/joshua-15-commentary

**v. 6**
- **Stone of Bohan.** Nobody knows what it commemorated, and commentators guess differently:
  - Jamieson-Fausset-Brown: the grave marker of a brave Reubenite leader killed in the conquest. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfb/joshua-15.html
  - Barnes: perhaps a memorial of some brave deed, but its site is "wholly uncertain." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/joshua/15-6.htm
  - Gill: three options — a gravestone, a memorial of an exploit, or (following the rabbi Kimchi) simply a boundary marker. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/joshua/15-6.htm
  - Utley (bible.org): it may have been only a boundary marker, not a memorial. https://bible.org/seriespage/joshua-15

**v. 7**
- **Valley of Achor.** This is where Achan was put to death (Joshua 7). A Bible Hub note reads it as a lasting lesson: obedience brings blessing and disobedience brings trouble. https://biblehub.com/joshua/15-7.htm
- **"Went up."** Madvig (on Precept Austin) says "up" and "down" refer to height, not north and south: the border climbs from the Dead Sea area. https://www.preceptaustin.org/joshua-15-commentary
- **This Debir is a different place.** Gill and Poole both say it is not Caleb's Debir near Hebron (vv. 15–17). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/joshua/15-7.htm
- **Which Gilgal? (disputed)**
  - Keil, Gill and the Cambridge Bible think this is not Israel's first camp near Jericho. They take it to be the Geliloth of Joshua 18:17.
  - The Pulpit Commentary, following Ewald, sees no reason to doubt it is the first camp.
  - https://biblehub.com/commentaries/joshua/15-7.htm
- **Adummim.** Barnes says the name means "red." Jerome explained it by the frequent bloodshed of robbers there, and the road is the setting of the Good Samaritan parable. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/joshua/15-7.htm

**v. 8**
- **Valley of Hinnom.**
  - The Preacher's Homiletical Commentary says this is the first time Scripture mentions the valley. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/joshua-15.html
  - Gill notes it later became notorious for child sacrifice to Moloch, and the New Testament word for hell, "Gehenna," comes from it. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/joshua/15-8.htm
- **Which tribe had Jerusalem? (disputed)**
  - Pulpit Commentary: Jerusalem lay north of the line, so it was in Benjamin.
  - Gill: part was probably in Judah and part in Benjamin, though Jewish writers often said it belonged to neither.
  - https://biblehub.com/commentaries/joshua/15-8.htm
  - Guzik: the city sat right on the Judah–Benjamin border. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-15-16-17/

**v. 12**
- Guzik says God gave out the land by tribe, clan and family, and the family was the most basic unit of God's people. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-15-16-17/

**v. 13**
- **Why "according to the LORD's command."** Matthew Henry says Joshua would not hand Caleb his portion outside the lot without God's instruction, even for an old friend. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Jos/Jos_015.cfm

**v. 14**
- **Were these the same giants the spies saw 45 years earlier?**
  - Gill: yes, the very same men. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/joshua/15-14.htm
  - Ellicott: the three names may be clans of the Anakim. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/erv/joshua/15-14.html
  - Pulpit Commentary: the phrase shouldn't be pressed literally; they may have been three chiefs. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/joshua/15-14.htm
- **When did this happen?**
  - The Geneva Study Bible puts it after Joshua's death (Judges 1:10). Gill thinks it was before.
  - Keil sees no conflict with Judges 1:10, which credits Judah: Caleb fought as head of a family, with their help.
  - https://biblehub.com/commentaries/joshua/15-14.htm
- **How it fits with Joshua 11:21–22.** Precept Austin's note suggests the Anakim may have moved back in after the first conquest. https://www.preceptaustin.org/joshua-15-commentary
- **Application.** Jamieson-Fausset-Brown say the victory was the reward of Caleb's trust in God. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/joshua/15-14.htm

**vv. 15–16**
- The prize Caleb offers suggests Debir was a strong, hard-to-take city. Keil and Delitzsch compare Saul's offer of his daughter to whoever killed Goliath. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/joshua/15-16.htm
- Benson adds that the offer assumed a lawful match and Achsah's consent. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/joshua/15-16.htm
- Guzik: Caleb did bold deeds himself and also encouraged others to do them. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-15-16-17/

**v. 17**
- Howard (quoted by Guzik) says Othniel was Caleb's nephew, so the land stayed in the family, and Othniel later became a judge (Judges 3:9–11). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-15-16-17/
- Precept Austin's note says the law did not forbid marrying a niece or cousin. https://www.preceptaustin.org/joshua-15-commentary
- Gill suggests Achsah may have been Caleb's daughter by a concubine (1 Chronicles 2:48). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/joshua/15-16.htm

**vv. 18–19**
- **Plain sense.** Coffman reads "land in the Negev" as "a dry estate," which is why she asked for springs. https://studylight.org/commentaries/bcc/joshua-15.html
- **The word "springs."** Madvig (quoted by Guzik) says the Hebrew word may mean "reservoirs" or "cisterns." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-15-16-17/
- **Link to Rebekah.** Hess (quoted by Constable) notes the scene echoes Rebekah coming to Isaac (Genesis 24), and both stories involve the blessing promised to Abraham. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/joshua/15-16.html
- **Achsah as a model of prayer.** Guzik lists several marks: she planned her request, asked humbly yet eagerly, kept it simple, and mixed thanks into her asking. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-15-16-17/
- **Matthew Henry's practical lessons.**
  - Desiring this life's comforts in moderation, by fair means, does not break the tenth commandment.
  - Husbands and wives should agree together about what is good for the family.
  - https://www.studylight.org/commentary/joshua/15-16.html
- **Allegorical readings.**
  - Henry notes a common use of the verse in prayer: "upper springs" for spiritual blessings, "lower springs" for bodily ones. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/joshua/15-16.html
  - Hawker sees the Holy Spirit veiling spiritual blessings in the gift. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/pmc/joshua-15.html
  - Gaebelein: "It is faith which asks much and receives much." https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/gab/joshua-15.html
  - Meyer (quoted by Guzik) compares it to Christ overcoming death and then giving the Church the springs. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-15-16-17/
- **A dissenting voice.** Dale Ralph Davis (on Precept Austin) says the chapter is profitable as it stands, "without spicing it up with any spiritualising additives." The Precept Austin editor's own aside on Henry's lines is "be a Berean." https://www.preceptaustin.org/joshua-15-commentary

**vv. 20–21**
- Guzik notes that many readers count 38 cities in the southern list, not the 29 the text gives. Clarke explains that nine were soon given to Simeon. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-15-16-17/
- Precept Austin cites Joshua 19:9: Judah's share was too large, so Simeon's inheritance was placed inside it. https://www.preceptaustin.org/joshua-15-commentary

**Differences between Protestant traditions**
I found no point where the traditions actually take opposite sides. Gill (labelled Baptist/Calvinist) and Wesley's Notes (labelled Arminian) both give plain historical readings of v. 14, and Wesley simply takes "drove thence" as driving them from their caves and forts. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/erv/joshua/15-14.html. The real disagreements are among individual commentators, not along denominational lines: the timing of Caleb's conquest (v. 14), which Gilgal is meant (v. 7), whether Jerusalem belonged to Judah or Benjamin (v. 8), and how far to spiritualise vv. 18–19.

**Other views**
- I found no Catholic, Orthodox, NET Bible note, Bible Odyssey, or prosperity/word-of-faith material on these verses.
- The only Brethren-style allegorical example I found is Kingcomments. It reads Anak as a picture of Satan and his three sons as everything in the world that rebels against God. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kng/joshua-15.html
